questions.q: Why does OWASP maintain a separate API Security Top 10 instead of relying solely on the main OWASP Top 10?
options: Because APIs fail in their own characteristic ways, mostly centered on object- and function-level authorization, that don't map cleanly onto page-rendering-focused issues like reflected XSS
Because the API Security Top 10 is identical to the main Top 10 and exists only for marketing reasons
Because APIs cannot be penetration tested at all
Because GraphQL APIs are immune to the risks in the main OWASP Top 10
questions.explain: Most of the main OWASP Top 10's web-focused language doesn't map cleanly onto a JSON request/response API. The API Security Top 10 instead centers on authorization failures specific to how APIs expose objects and functions.

questions.q: What is the exact test that confirms a Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA) vulnerability?
options: Checking whether the API responds over HTTPS
Sending a malformed JSON body and checking for a 500 error
Authenticating as User A, noting an object's ID, then replaying that same request while authenticated as User B to see if User B can access User A's object
Measuring how fast the API responds to a single request
questions.explain: BOLA is confirmed by swapping an authenticated session: if User B's session can read or modify an object (like an order ID) that actually belongs to User A, the API checked authentication but never checked object ownership.

questions.q: What is mass assignment, in the context of an API endpoint like PATCH /api/users/me?
options: An API returning too many results in a single paginated response
An endpoint blindly binding every field in a submitted JSON body to a backend object, letting unexposed fields like "role" or "accountBalance" be set even though the UI never offered them
An API accepting requests from too many different IP addresses at once
A database allowing bulk inserts of more than 1,000 rows
questions.explain: Mass assignment happens when the backend maps an entire submitted body onto a record instead of allow-listing fields, so adding fields like role or accountBalance to the request body can set them even though no UI control exposed them.

questions.q: Why is missing or weak rate limiting classified as its own OWASP API Security Top 10 category (Unrestricted Resource Consumption) rather than treated purely as a performance concern?
options: Because rate limiting has no relationship to security whatsoever
Because rate limiting is only relevant to GraphQL APIs, not REST
Because APIs without rate limiting always crash immediately
Because its absence directly enables brute-forcing reset codes, mass user-ID enumeration, or running up cost on metered backend resources
questions.explain: Unrestricted Resource Consumption exists because missing rate limiting is directly exploitable — it enables brute force, large-scale enumeration against vulnerable endpoints, and cost-based abuse of metered backends like AI inference or SMS sending.

questions.q: A GraphQL API's updateUser mutation accepts an input type with more fields than any client UI ever sends in practice. What should a tester do?
options: Assume GraphQL mutations are safe by design and skip testing them
Test the mutation the same way as a REST mass-assignment check: submit extra fields from the schema that the UI never exposed and see if they take effect
Only test GraphQL queries, never mutations
Report it as a finding automatically without testing, since extra fields in a schema are always exploitable
questions.explain: GraphQL mutations need the same mass-assignment scrutiny as REST endpoints: submit extra fields drawn from the schema that the UI never sends, and check whether the backend applies them anyway.
